## Categorical Data Analysis
In this lab, we will study some contingency tables using the Chi-Squared Test and Fisher's Exact Test.

## Chi-Squared Test
Examine the following table showing data on how much students studied for their Calculus final and their final exam grade for randomly selected students at a large state school.  These are our observed cell counts.
```{webr-r}
Observed = matrix(c(6,6,8,10,11,6,13,14,8,7,11,10,6,6,6), ncol=5, byrow=TRUE)
colnames(Observed) = c("A","B","C","D","F")
rownames(Observed) = c(" Not Much"," A Few Hours", "A Few Days")
Observed = as.table(Observed)
Observed
```


Now we plot the distribution of grades for each category of time spent studying. Does it look like the marginal distributions are the same?
```{webr-r}
# Creating a side-by-side barplot
barplot(t(Observed), 
        beside = TRUE, 
        main = "Distribution of Scores by Time Studied", 
        xlab = "Time Studied", 
        ylab = "Frequency",
        col = c("darkgreen", "lightgreen", "khaki", "orange", "firebrick"),
        ylim = c(0, 20), # Adjust y-limit to fit the legend cleanly
        legend.text = colnames(Observed),
        args.legend = list(title = "Grades", x = "topleft"))
```

Now, we will find the expected cell counts using the row and column sums.  Remember the formula is
$$\frac{\text{Row Sum}\cdot \text{Column Sum}}{\text{Total Sample Size}} $$

```{webr-r}
# Calculating Expected Cell Counts
# Get row totals, column totals, and the total sample size
row_sum = rowSums(Observed)
col_sum = colSums(Observed)
total_size = sum(Observed)

# Calculate expected counts using the outer product of row and col totals
Expected = outer(row_sum, col_sum) / total_size

# Re-assign names so the table is easy to read
rownames(Expected) = rownames(Observed)
colnames(Expected) = colnames(Observed)

print("Expected Cell Counts (Manual Calculation):")
print(Expected)
```


Now let's perform a Chi-Squared Test of independence on this data.  We will use $\alpha = 0.05$.  First let's calculate our test statistic.
```{webr-r}

#  Calculate the chi-squared components for each cell
# This applies the formula (O - E)^2 / E to every cell in the table simultaneously
chi_components <- (Observed - Expected)^2 / Expected

print("Individual Cell Contributions to Chi-Squared:")
print(round(chi_components, 4))

# Sum them all together to get the final test statistic
chi_sq_statistic <- sum(chi_components)

print("--------------------------------------------------")
print(paste("Final Manual Chi-Squared Statistic:", round(chi_sq_statistic, 4)))

```

Now let's find the P-value for our test statistic:
```{webr-r}
# Get degrees of freedom
df = (nrow(Observed)-1)*(ncol(Expected)-1)
P.val = pchisq(chi_sq_statistic, df, lower.tail = FALSE)
print("P-value is ")
print(round(P.val, 4))

```

The resulting P-value exceeds our chosen level of significance $\alpha$, leading us to **fail to reject the null hypothesis**. Consequently, there is insufficient evidence to suggest a statistically significant association between final exam grades and the amount of time spent studying. Note that failing to reject the null hypothesis does not explicitly prove the variables are entirely independent, only that this current sample did not provide strong enough evidence to detect a relationship.

## The chisq.test( ) Function
Now that you have learned how to run the Chi-Squared test manually, you are now ready to fully automate this using a built-in R function.
```{webr-r}
print(chisq.test(Observed))

```
We should get the same P-value and test statistic as above.  

## Fisher's Exact Test
As we learned in lecture, the Chi-Squared test in an asymptotic test.  This means it is only valid if all expected cell counts are greater than 5.  But what do we do if some cell counts in our table are less than 5? In this, case we will use Fisher's Exact Test.  

```{webr-r}
# First try Fisher's Exact Test on our previous data to see if we get the same result. 
Observed = matrix(c(6,6,8,10,11,6,13,14,8,7,11,10,6,6,6), ncol=5, byrow=TRUE)
print(fisher.test(Observed))
```


```{webr-r}
# Now let's make the values lower in the talbe and rerun both tests
Observed2 = matrix(c(1,1,7,7,7,1,6,7,6,7,7,4,1,1,1), ncol=5, byrow=TRUE)
print(chisq.test(Observed2)) # NOTE: you should get a warning when you run this line.
print(fisher.test(Observed2))
```
How do the P-values differ between the tests? Which test would be more reliable for this data?


## Goodness of Fit Tests (GOF)
Another common scenario where the chi-squared statistic can be used is checking to see if a proposed theoretical model of a probability distribution agrees with an observed sample of the distribution.  

Let’s imagine a candy company claims that their bags contain a specific theoretical distribution of three colors: 50% Red, 30% Green, and 20% Blue.

You buy a large bag, count out 100 candies, and find the following observed frequencies:

45 Red

35 Green

20 Blue

We want to test if your observed bag fits their theoretical model.
```{webr-r}
# 1. Define your observed data (1 row of counts for 3 categories)
observed_counts = c(45, 35, 20)
names(observed_counts) = c("Red", "Green", "Blue")

# 2. Define the theoretical probabilities according to the model
# NOTE: These probabilities must add up exactly to 1.0.
theoretical_probs = c(0.50, 0.30, 0.20)

# 3. Run the Chi-Squared Goodness of Fit test
# 'x' is your observed data, 'p' is your theoretical model
gof_test = chisq.test(x = observed_counts, p = theoretical_probs)

# 4. Print the test results
print("Goodness of Fit Test Results:")
print(gof_test)

```
What is the conclusion of this test? Is the company's theoretical candy model supported by our observed bag?
